1	/*
2	 * persistent.h
3	 *
4	 * This is the structure for the data that we store in the "InfoA" section of flash memory. This data persists through power cycles.
5	 * We break it out into a header file solely so that the ASM code can include it to find the address of `mins`, which the ISR needs to increment once per minute.
6	 *
7	 *  Created on: Jul 18, 2024
8	 *      Author: passp
9	 */
10	
11	#ifndef PERSISTENT_H_
12	#define PERSISTENT_H_
13	
14	#include "timeblock.h"
15	
16	// Here is the persistent data that we store in "information memory" FRAM that survives power cycles
17	// and reprogramming.
18	
19	struct __attribute__((__packed__)) persistent_data_t {
20	
21	    rv3032_time_block_t programmed_time;        // Calendar time when this unit was Programmed. Used to initialize the RTC on first power up.
22	    rv3032_time_block_t launched_time;          // Time when this unit was launched relative to programmed time. Set when trigger pulled, never read.
23	
24	
25	    // State. We have 3 persistent states, (1) first startup fresh from factory programming, (2) ready to launch, (3) launched.
26	    // We make these volatile to ensure that the compiler actually writes changes to memory rather than trying to cache in a register
27	
28	    volatile unsigned initalized_flag;                         // Set to 1 by program fixture after successfully power test. If !1, then we show "TEST".
29	    volatile unsigned commisisoned_flag;                       // Set to 1 after we commission, which involves inserting the batteries and trigger pin. This is when we set the RTC to the programmed time.
30	    volatile unsigned launched_flag;                           // Set to 1 when the trigger pin is pulled.
31	
32	    volatile unsigned porsoltCount;                            // How many 0.1 seconds did the unit stay alive after power was removed during initialization?
33	
34	    volatile unsigned tsl_powerup_count;                           // How many times have we booted up since we initialized (Max 65535. Should be 1 until first battery change in about 150 years.)
35	
36	    // Time since launch
37	    volatile unsigned mins;             // It would be too much work to update this every second, so once a minute is good. Note that it is possible for this value to end up at `minutes_per_day`, in which case you must normalize it and increment days.
38	    volatile unsigned long days;        // Has to be long since 2^16 days is only ~180 years and we plan on working for much longer than that.
39	
40	    // We need to be able to update the above values atomically so we use an interlock here so we can do the right thing in case we get interrupted exactly in the middle of an update.
41	    volatile unsigned update_flag;             // Set to 1 when an update is in progress (backup values are valid)
42	    volatile unsigned backup_mins;             // These backup values are captured before we set `update_flag`.
43	    volatile unsigned long backup_days;
44	
45	};

48	// This area of memory never gets overwritten, not by power cycle and not by downloading a new binary image into program FRAM.

50	extern persistent_data_t persistent_data;

			ADD.B		#1,R10						; Increment hours. TODO: We could use an ADD.B here and then use overlfow flag to avoid the CMP

			CMP			#10,R10
			JGE			HOURS_GE_10

			; If we get here then incremented hours is 1-9
			; Display the hours 1 digit
			MOV.B		hours_lcd_bytes(R10),&(LCDM0W_L+13)		; Display hours in the hours ones digit on the LCD. Remember that the hours table is *not* offset like secs and mins.

			JMP 		TSL_DONE					; This wastes 3 cycles every hour, we could just repeat the ending motif here.

HOURS_GE_10
			CMP			#20,R10
			JGE			HOURS_GE_20

			; If we get here then incremented hours is 10-19

			; We could save a couple of cycles here by only displaying the tens digit if hours is equal to "10"
			MOV.B		&(hours_lcd_bytes+1),&(LCDM0W_L+10)			; Display "1" in hours 10's digit
			MOV.B		(hours_lcd_bytes-10)(R10),&(LCDM0W_L+13)	; Display hours 1's digit in the hours ones digit on the LCD (see what I did there? :) )

			JMP 		TSL_DONE					; This wastes 3 cycles every hour, we could just repeat the ending motif here.

HOURS_GE_20

			CMP			#24,R10
			JGE			HOURS_EQ_24

			; If we get here then incremented hours is 20-23

			MOV.B		&(hours_lcd_bytes+2),&(LCDM0W_L+10)			; Display "2" in hours 10's digit
			MOV.B		(hours_lcd_bytes-20)(R10),&(LCDM0W_L+13)	; Display hours 1's digit in the hours ones digit on the LCD (see what I did there? :) )

			JMP 		TSL_DONE					; This wastes 3 cycles every hour, we could just repeat the ending motif here.


HOURS_EQ_24

			; If we get here then incremented hours is 24 so we have to roll to next day

			MOV.W		#0, R10			; Reset hours to 0

			MOV.B		&(hours_lcd_bytes+0),&(LCDM0W_L+13)			; Display "0" in hours 10's digit
			MOV.B		&(hours_lcd_bytes+0),&(LCDM0W_L+10)			; Display "0" in hours 1's digit


			PUSH.W		R11											; R11-R14 are not callee saved, so we have to save them before calling C.
			PUSH.W		R12
			CALL		#tsl_new_day								; Call the C++ side for a new day. Updates the days digits on the LCD and atomically
																	; (increments the persistant days and clears the minutes).
			POP.W		R12											; TODO: We could just reload the orginal values here and save a PUSH/POP.
			POP.W		R11

TSL_DONE
;----------------------------------------------------------------------
; 900 | CBI( RV3032_CLKOUT_PIFG , RV3032_CLKOUT_B );      // Clear the pending
;     | RV3032 INT interrupt flag that got us into this ISR.
;----------------------------------------------------------------------

        	;This is the standard way to clear the interrupt flag
        	;BIC.B     #2,&PAIFG_L+0         ; Clear the interrupt flag that got us here

        	;Here we save a cycle with a constant-sourced move. We can do this becuase we know a priori that once we enter TSL mode that

        	MOV.B     #0,&PAIFG_L+0         ; Clear the interrupt flag that got us here

 	  		;AND.B     #127,&PAOUT_L+0       ; Clear DEBUGA for profiling purposes.

            reti							; pops previous sleep mode, so puts us back to sleep
            								; TODO: Replace this IRET with a sleep and save 4 cycles, and then
            								; just clear 60 PUSHes off the stack every minute with a single write to SP.

            .sect   PORT1_VECTOR             ; Vector
            .short  TSL_MODE_ISR             ;


;---- RTL ISR RAMFUNC
; 48us
; 26us startup after CLKOUT from FRAM
; 1.33uA

;---- RTL SQUIGLLE ISR FRAM
; 51us
; 28us startup after CLKOUT from FRAM
; 1.35uA

;Begin the RTL mode ISR
;Set the ISR vector to point here to start this mode.
;Assumes the symbol `ready_to_launch_lcd_frames` points to a table of LCD frames for the squiggle animation

		.text								; We need to switch back to text section becuase the above ISR definition chnages to the ISR section. :/

		.global  	RTL_MODE_BEGIN			; Publish function address so C can call it.

RTL_MODE_BEGIN:
	;This entry point sets up all the registers and changes the PORT_1 vector to point to the optimized ISR, which will get called directly on subsequent interrupts
	;First we update the vector to point to the recurring ISR vector
	mov.w	#RTL_MODE_ISR, &ram_vector_PORT1

	;For MSP430 and MSP430X, the ABI designates R4-R10 as callee-saved registers. That is, a called function is
	;expected to preserve them so they have the same value on return from a function as they had at the point of the
	;call.

	mov.w	#ready_to_launch_lcd_frame_words,R12 		; Save the address of the base of the table. We will use this as a live pointer.
	mov.w	#(128-1),R13 								; We will use this for a 1 cycle, no branch way to normalize our pointer which by luck is into an 8*(8*2) table
	mov.w	R12,R14										; Keep a copy of the base address to OR in later


	;; Disable the FRAM controller
	; With controller on uses 1.36uA
	; With controller off uses 1.37uA
	; Why?
	; MOV.W	#FRCTLPW,&FRCTL0			; Write password to FRAM controller
	; BIC.W	#FRPWR,&GCCTL0				; Clear the bit that turns on the controller on wake

	; We are now ready, so drop into the real ISR. The real ISR will be called directly for now on since we updated the vector to point here.

; This is the entry point for the ISR
; We leave this mode when the trigger is pulled by the trigger ISR

RTL_MODE_ISR:

 	; OR.B      #128,&PAOUT_L+0  ;			// DebugA ON - For profiling

	; Copy the data for this frame into the LCDMEM registers.
	; note only need to do this for the LPINs that are actually connected,
	; which are the only ones we put into the table.
	; note we can do this 4 nibbles at a time for free using .W instructions.

      MOV.W @R12+,(LCDM0W_L+0)		; L0,L1,L2,L3 - 4 cycles
      MOV.W @R12+,(LCDM0W_L+2)		; L4,L5,L6,L7
	;					   +4		; L8,L9,L10,L11  (These are the COM pins, do not want to mess with them)
      MOV.W @R12+,(LCDM0W_L+6)		; L12,L13,L14,L15
      MOV.W @R12+,(LCDM0W_L+8)		; L16,L17,L18,L19
      MOV.W @R12+,(LCDM0W_L+10)		; L20,L21,L22,L23
      MOV.W @R12+,(LCDM0W_L+12)		; L24,L25,L26,L27
      MOV.W @R12+,(LCDM0W_L+14)		; L28,L29,L30,L31
      MOV.W @R12+,(LCDM0W_L+16)		; L32,L33,L34,L35

      AND.W R13,R12					; Look ma, no compare/branch/load! 1 cycle each AND and OR.
      OR.W  R14,R12					; OR back in the base address (remember it is 128 byte aligned)


      BIC.B     #2,&PAIFG_L+0 ;  	; Clear interrupt flag
      								; Note that we can not use the constant-MOV 0x00 trick that worked above becuase
      								; in RTL mode the person could pull the trigger, which would set the flag for that pin and if
      								; we then hd bad timing and cleared that bit here then the pull would be lost forever.

 	  ; AND.B     #127,&PAOUT_L+0       ; DEBUGA OFF - For profiling

      RETI

;------------------------------------------------------------------------------
;           Interrupt Vectors
;------------------------------------------------------------------------------

            .end

146	static unsigned char USI_TWI_Write_Byte( unsigned char data ) {
147	
148	    for( uint8_t bitMask=0b10000000; bitMask !=0; bitMask>>=1 ) {

150	        // setup data bit

152	        if ( data & bitMask) {

195	static unsigned char i2c_start( unsigned char slave , unsigned char readFlag) {
196

198

202	    // SCL is high, is defined to be a START condition or a repeated start condition.
203	
204	    sda_drive_low();
205	
206	    _delay_us(BIT_TIME_US);
207	
208	    scl_drive_low();
209	
210	    // A START condition is always followed by the (unique) 7-bit slave address (MSB first) and then w/r bit
211	
212	    // The control word is latched internally on
213	    // rising SCLK edges and is eight bits in length, comprised
214	    // of a seven bit device address equal to 0010000b and a
215	    // read/write bit (write = 0 and read = 1).

319	    unsigned char *buffer = (unsigned char *)in_buffer;
320	
321	    i2c_start( slave , 0 );      // "CPU transmits the RX8900's slave address with the R/W bit set to write mode."

324	
325	    // Write returns with SDA high (ACK bit released), SCL low.
326	
327	    // We are doing a restart here, so force clock high, then Start() will pull sda low with clock high
328	
329	    scl_drive_high();
330	    _delay_us(BIT_TIME_US);
331	    _delay_us(BIT_TIME_US);
332	    _delay_us(BIT_TIME_US);
333	
334	    i2c_start( slave , 1 );      // "CPU transfers RESTART condition [Sr] (in which case, CPU does not transfer a STOP condition [P])"
335	
336	    // SCL low
337	
338	    while (count) {
339	
340	        unsigned char data=0;
341	
342	        for( uint8_t bitMask=0b10000000; bitMask !=0; bitMask>>=1 ) {
343	
344	            // Clock in the data bits
345	
346	            scl_drive_high();           // Clock in the first data bit
347	
348	            _delay_us(BIT_TIME_US);
349	
350	            if (sda_read()) {
351	
352	                data |= bitMask;
353	
354	            }
355	
356	            scl_drive_low();
357	
358	            _delay_us(BIT_TIME_US);
359	
360	        }
361	
362	        // SCLK low here
363	        // SDA should be pulled high and not driven low by the FMIC because
364	        // we are reading so it is our turn to ACK now
365	
366	        *buffer = data;
367	
368	        buffer++;
369	
370	        count--;

373	
374	            //After each byte of data is read,
375	            //the controller IC must drive an acknowledge (SDIO = 0)
376	            //if an additional byte of data will be requested. Data
377	            //transfer ends with the STOP condition.
378	
379	            sda_drive_low();            // drive SDA to ACK that we read the byte
380	            _delay_us(BIT_TIME_US);     // Not needed, but so we can see what is happening on the scope
381	
382	
383	            scl_drive_high();            // Clock out the ACK bit
384	            _delay_us(BIT_TIME_US);
385	
386	            scl_drive_low();
387	            _delay_us(BIT_TIME_US);     // Not necessary
388	            sda_pull_high();            // Back to normal condition pulling SDA high (slave will have next data bit on bus now)
389	            _delay_us(BIT_TIME_US);
390	
391	            // Ready for next bit..
392	
393	        }
394	    }
395	
396	    // Ok, we got all the bits we need.
397	    // We did not send a ACK on the last byte, so
398	    // SCL is still low from the final data bit.
399	    // SDA is pulled high because the slave is waiting for use to drive low to ACK (we will STOP instead)
400	
401	    /*
402	        FROM TI:
403	
404	        "Once the master has received the number of bytes it is expecting, it
405	        will send a NACK, signaling to the slave to halt communications and release the bus. The master will
406	        follow this up with a STOP condition."
407	
408	        https://www.google.com/url?sa=t&rct=j&q=&esrc=s&source=web&cd=1&cad=rja&uact=8&ved=0ahUKEwj9mr_HuobYAhVJON8KHfV0CeMQFggoMAA&url=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.ti.com%2Flit%2Fan%2Fslva704%2Fslva704.pdf&usg=AOvVaw0MO8lWY9iHs3PZqsN6fgWm
409	
410	        From FM_IC Daata sheet:
411	
412	        "After each byte of data is read,
413	        the controller IC must drive an acknowledge (SDIO = 0)
414	        if an additional byte of data will be requested. Data
415	        transfer ends with the STOP condition. After every
416	        STOP condition, the internal address counter is reset."
417	
418	        This actually makes sense if you consider the case where the high bit in the
419	        next data byte being read is a 0. In this case, the FM_IC will hold the SDA line LOW
420	        after the ACK bit is clocked, making it impossible to send the stop condition.
421	
422	        This actually happened in the wild when issuing a WRITE to do a seek after issuing a
423	        RED to get he the currently tuned station for a save.
424	
425	    */
426	
427	    scl_drive_high();            // SDA is is high, so we are clocking out a NAK
428	    _delay_us(BIT_TIME_US);
429	    scl_drive_low();            // finish clocking out a NAK
430	
431	    i2c_stop();
432	
433	    // End transaction with bus in idle
434	
435	    return(0);
436	
437	}

200	     */

202	    // Note that we do not enable the CLKOUT interrupt until we enter RTL or TSL mode
203	
204	    // --- Trigger
205	
206	    // By default we set the trigger to drive low so it will not use power regardless if the pin is in or out.
207	    // When the trigger is out, the pin is shorted to ground.
208	    // We will switch it to pull-up later if we need to (because we have not launched yet).
209

214	    // switch to ready-to-lanch mode when the trigger is inserted at the factory. The interrupt will then get
215	    // disabled again and the pull up will get disabled after the trigger is pulled since once that happens we
216	    // dont care about the trigger state anymore and we don't want to waste power with either the pull-up getting shorted to ground

542	// Called when trigger pin changes high to low, indicating the trigger has been pulled and we should start ticking.
543	// Note that this interrupt is only enabled when we enter ready-to-launch mode, and then it is disabled and also the pin in driven low
544	// when we then switch to time-since-lanuch mode, so this ISR can only get called in ready-to-lanuch mode.
545	
546	__interrupt void trigger_isr(void) {
547	
548	    DEBUG_PULSE_ON();
549	
550	    // First we delay for about 1000 cycles / 1.1Mhz  = ~1ms
551	    // This will filter glitches since the pin will not still be low when we sample it after this delay. We want to be really sure!
552	    __delay_cycles( 1000 );
553	
554	    // Then clear any interrupt flag that got us here.
555	    // Timing here is critical, we must clear the flag *before* we capture the pin state or we might miss a change
556	    CBI( TRIGGER_PIFG , TRIGGER_B );      // Clear any pending trigger pin interrupt flag
557	
558	    // Grab the current trigger pin level
559	    unsigned triggerpin_level = TBI( TRIGGER_PIN , TRIGGER_B );
560	
561	    // Now we can check to see if the trigger pin was still low
562	    // If it is not still low then we will return and this ISR will get called again if it goes low again or
563	    // if it went low between when we cleared the flag and when we sampled it (VERY small race window of only 1/8th of a microsecond, but hey we need to be perfect, it could be a once in a lifetime moment and we dont want to miss it!)
564	
565	    if ( !triggerpin_level ) {      // trigger still pulled?
566	
567	        // WE HAVE LIFTOFF!
568	
569	        // Disable the trigger pin and drive low to save power and prevent any more interrupts from it
570	        // (if it stayed pulled up then it would draw power though the pull-up resistor whenever the pin was out)
571	
572	        CBI( TRIGGER_POUT , TRIGGER_B );      // low
573	        SBI( TRIGGER_PDIR , TRIGGER_B );      // drive
574	
575	        CBI( TRIGGER_PIFG , TRIGGER_B );      // Clear any pending interrupt (it could have gone high again since we sampled it). We already triggered so we don't care anymore.
576	
577	        // Show all 0's on the LCD to quickly let the user know that we saw the pull
578	        lcd_show_zeros();
579	
580	        // Do the actual launch, which will...
581	        // 1. Read the current RTC time and save it to FRAM
582	        // 2. Set the launchflag in FRAM so we will forevermore know that we did launch already.
583	        // 3. Reset the current RTC time to midnight 1/1/00.
584	
585	        // Initialize our i2c pins as pull-up
586	        i2c_init();
587	
588	        unlock_persistant_data();
589	        // First get current time and save it to FRAM for archival purposes.
590	        i2c_read( RV_3032_I2C_ADDR , RV3032_SECS_REG  , (void *)  &persistent_data.launched_time , sizeof( rv3032_time_block_t ) );
591	        // Also update the persistent storage to reflect that we launched now.
592	        persistent_data.mins=0;
593	        persistent_data.days=0;
594	        persistent_data.update_flag=0;
595	        persistent_data.launched_flag=0x01;
596	        lock_persistant_data();
597	
598	        // Then zero out the RTC to start counting over again, starting now. Note that writing any value to the seconds register resets the sub-second counters to the beginning of the second.
599	        // "Writing to the Seconds register creates an immediate positive edge on the LOW signal on CLKOUT pin."

600	        i2c_write( RV_3032_I2C_ADDR , RV3032_SECS_REG  , &rv_3032_time_block_init , sizeof( rv3032_time_block_t ) );
601	
602	        i2c_shutdown();
603	
604	        // Note that the tsl_* variables will already be initialized to zero from power up
605	
606	        // We will get the next tick with a rising edge on CLKOUT in 1000ms. Make sure we return from this ISR before then.
607	
608	        // Clear any pending RTC interrupt so we will not tick until the next pulse comes from RTC in 1000ms
609	        // There could be a race where an RTC interrupt comes in just after the trigger was pulled, in which case we would
610	        // have a pending interrupt that would get serviced immediately after we return from here, which would look ugly.
611	        // We could also see an interrupt if the CLKOUT signal was low when trigger pulled (50% likelihood) since it will go high on reset.
612	
613	        CBI( RV3032_CLKOUT_PIFG , RV3032_CLKOUT_B );      // Clear any pending interrupt from CLKOUT
614	
615	        // Flash lights
616	
617	        flash();
618	
619	        // Start ticking from... now!
620	        // (We rely on the secs, mins, hours, and days_digits[] all having been init'ed to zeros.)
621	
622	        // Begin TSL mode on next tick
623	        SET_CLKOUT_VECTOR( &TSL_MODE_BEGIN );
624	
625	    }
626	
627	    DEBUG_PULSE_OFF();
628

## Deep Code Review: TSL-calibre-MSP

### 1. CLKOUT busy-wait has no timeout - can drain battery permanently
**File:** `tsl-calibre-msp.cpp:1468-1469`
```cpp
unsigned start_val = TBI( RV3032_CLKOUT_PIN, RV3032_CLKOUT_B );
while (TBI( RV3032_CLKOUT_PIN, RV3032_CLKOUT_B )==start_val); // wait for any transition
```
If the RV3032 fails to produce CLKOUT transitions (I2C misconfiguration, defective chip, broken trace), this spins forever at full CPU current (~200uA at 1MHz). For a device designed to last centuries on a battery, this turns a recoverable RTC failure into a dead battery. A timeout falling into `error_mode()` would be much safer.

---

### 2. All I2C return values silently ignored
**File:** `i2c_master.cpp` / `tsl-calibre-msp.cpp`

Every I2C function returns a status (ACK/NACK) but no caller ever checks it:
```cpp
i2c_start( slave , 0 );      // TODO: check for error   (line 254, 285)
USI_TWI_Write_Byte( addr );  // TODO: CHeck ret         (line 183)
```
If the RV3032 doesn't ACK (cold solder joint, ESD damage, backup cap still charging), the entire RTC configuration is silently skipped - CLKOUT frequency, backup switchover, EEPROM refresh disable - all could be wrong. Combined with issue #1, this means a failed I2C transaction leads directly to infinite battery drain.

---

### 3. `trigger_isr()` never disables PORT2 interrupt enable
**File:** `tsl-calibre-msp.cpp:570-575`
```cpp
CBI( TRIGGER_POUT , TRIGGER_B );      // low
SBI( TRIGGER_PDIR , TRIGGER_B );      // drive
CBI( TRIGGER_PIFG , TRIGGER_B );      // Clear flag
// Missing: CBI( TRIGGER_PIE, TRIGGER_B );  -- PIE is still set!
```
After the trigger pull, the pin is driven low and the flag is cleared, but `TRIGGER_PIE` (P2IE bit 1) remains enabled. When `TSL_MODE_BEGIN` later switches to FRAM-based vectors (`BIC.W #SYSRIVECT,&SYSCTL`), there is no FRAM PORT2 vector defined in the codebase. If any hardware glitch ever sets P2IFG bit 1 (even EMI or a cosmic ray bit-flip - relevant over a century-scale lifetime), the CPU would vector to uninitialized FRAM (0xFFFF = reset vector), causing an unplanned restart. Adding `CBI( TRIGGER_PIE, TRIGGER_B )` is a one-instruction fix.

---

### 4. No post-launch RTC clock-loss validation on battery-change restart
**File:** `tsl-calibre-msp.cpp:1333-1456`, `error_codes.h:28`

`BATT_ERROR_POSTLAUNCH` is defined but never used. After a battery change during TSL mode, the code retrieves time from FRAM and resumes counting. But it never checks the RV3032's PORF/VLF flags to detect whether the oscillator stopped during the battery change. If the backup capacitor drained during a slow battery swap and the RV3032 oscillator stopped, CLKOUT may initially be unstable or at the wrong frequency after `rv3032_init()`. The code relies entirely on the 1100ms delay being sufficient, with no validation that CLKOUT is actually ticking at 1Hz.

---

### 5. `_BV(x)` macro missing parentheses around parameter
**File:** `util.h:14`
```cpp
#define _BV(x) (1<<x)     // should be (1<<(x))
```
If `_BV` is ever called with an expression like `_BV(a|b)`, operator precedence gives `(1 << a | b)` instead of `(1 << (a|b))`. Currently all call sites use simple constants, so this never manifests. But it's a latent defect that would be extremely hard to debug if it ever triggered.

---

### 6. DEBUGB pin configured with pull-up but never read / `testing_only_mode` is dead code
**File:** `tsl-calibre-msp.cpp:540`, `pins.h:114-121`

`testing_only_mode` is declared at line 540 but never set or checked. The DEBUGB pin is configured as input with pull-up enabled (lines 168-170) with the comment "Currently checked at power up, if low then we go into testonly mode" - but no code actually reads it. The pull-up draws ~50nA continuously, which is wasted. This appears to be an incomplete feature.

---

### 7. `tsl_secs/tsl_mins/tsl_hours` are `unsigned` (16-bit) but ASM reads them as bytes
**File:** `tsl-calibre-msp.cpp:525-527`, `tsl_asm.asm:42-59`

```cpp
unsigned tsl_secs=0;   // 16-bit
unsigned tsl_mins=0;
unsigned tsl_hours=0;
```
```asm
MOV.B &tsl_secs,R6    ; reads only low byte
MOV.B &tsl_mins,R9
MOV.B &tsl_hours,R10
```
The ASM comments say "stored as a byte on the C side" but they're actually `unsigned` (16-bit). This works because the values never exceed 59/59/23 (all fit in a byte), and MSP430 is little-endian so the low byte is at the variable's address. But it's fragile - if anyone adds code that sets `tsl_hours = 256` for any reason, the ASM would read 0.

---

### 8. DEBUGB pin definition mismatch vs. comment
**File:** `pins.h:114-121`

```cpp
// Debug out B on pin P8.3 which is pin number 19 on MSP430
#define DEBUGB_PREN P1REN
#define DEBUGB_PDIR P1DIR
#define DEBUGB_POUT P1OUT
```
Comment says "P8.3" but all macros map to P1 registers with bit 6. The comment is stale/wrong. If someone relies on the comment to find the physical pin, they'll look at the wrong port.

---

### 9. RV3032 INT pin: comment says INPUT, code makes it OUTPUT
**File:** `tsl-calibre-msp.cpp:177`
```cpp
SBI( RV3032_INT_PDIR , RV3032_INT_B ); // INPUT    <-- comment is wrong
```
`SBI` on `PDIR` sets the pin to OUTPUT, not input. The comment is backwards. The code itself is fine (driving the unused INT pin low to prevent it from floating), but the misleading comment could cause confusion during maintenance.

---

### 10. `CSCTL4 = 0` in centesimus dies assumes default register value
**File:** `tsl-calibre-msp.cpp:802`
```cpp
CSCTL4 = SELMS__VLOCLK;       // Switch to VLO
__delay_cycles(5000UL);
CSCTL4 = 0;                   // "Switch back to DCO"
```
Writing `0` to CSCTL4 assumes that's the correct running configuration. On MSP430FR4133, SELMS=0 does select DCOCLK, but this also sets SELA=0 (which selects XT1CLK for ACLK). If any code path ever changes ACLK source, this would silently break it. A save/restore pattern would be more robust.

---

### 11. `power_rundown_test()` and `batt_v_x1000()` are defined but never called
**File:** `tsl-calibre-msp.cpp:949-1161`

These functions and their supporting infrastructure (`POWERDOWN_TEST_ISR`, `adc_vcc_init`, `adc_measure`, `adc_shutdown`, `amps_hi_message`, `amps_lo_message`) are implemented but never invoked from any code path. This is ~200 lines of dead code in a micro-power embedded system where code size matters for FRAM usage.

---

### 12. VLO clock variability could stretch centesimus dies delay beyond 1 second
**File:** `tsl-calibre-msp.cpp:799-800`
```cpp
CSCTL4 = SELMS__VLOCLK;
__delay_cycles(5000UL);     // "half a second" at 10KHz
```
VLO on MSP430FR4133 can range from ~4KHz to ~20KHz depending on temperature and manufacturing variation. At 4KHz, this delay is 1.25 seconds, which exceeds the 1-second RTC tick interval. The pending tick would fire immediately after the ISR returns, so no seconds are permanently lost, but there would be a visible hitch in the displayed time. Cosmetic, not functional.

---

### 13. RTL_MODE_ISR comment about trigger flag clearing is misleading
**File:** `tsl_asm.asm:269-272`

The comment explains using `BIC.B` instead of `MOV.B #0` to avoid clearing the trigger pin's interrupt flag. But the trigger is on PORT2 (P2IFG) and CLKOUT is on PORT1 (P1IFG) - they're in completely different registers. The `MOV.B #0` on P1IFG can never affect the trigger flag in P2IFG. The `BIC.B` vs `MOV.B` choice is harmless (costs 1 extra cycle per tick) but the reasoning in the comment is incorrect.

---

### Summary

The top 3 actionable items:
1. Add a timeout to the CLKOUT busy-wait (issue #1) - prevents permanent battery drain on RTC failure
2. Add `CBI(TRIGGER_PIE, TRIGGER_B)` in `trigger_isr()` (issue #3) - prevents undefined behavior from glitch-triggered PORT2 interrupt after FRAM vector switch
3. Check at least the I2C ACK on the critical CLKOUT frequency configuration write (issue #2) - validate the RTC is responding before depending on it
